claim: Otto Warburg first described aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells over 90 years ago.
source: Although Otto Warburg first described aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells >90 years ago, the primary purpose of this metabolic switch remains controversial.
evidence: This is a historical reference to Warburg's work, supported by citations in the manuscript (Warburg et al., 1927; Warburg et al., 1924).

claim: The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway requires glucose and glutamine for de novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc.
source: The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway requires glucose and glutamine for de novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc, a sugar-nucleotide that inhibits receptor endocytosis and signaling by promoting N-acetylglucosamine branching of Asn (N)-linked glycans.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the hexosamine pathway.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc inhibits receptor endocytosis and signaling by promoting N-acetylglucosamine branching of N-linked glycans.
source: The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway requires glucose and glutamine for de novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc, a sugar-nucleotide that inhibits receptor endocytosis and signaling by promoting N-acetylglucosamine branching of Asn (N)-linked glycans.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis cooperatively reduce UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis and N-glycan branching in mouse T cell blasts by starving the hexosamine pathway of glucose and glutamine.
source: Here, we report that aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis co-operatively reduce UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis and N-glycan branching in mouse T cell blasts by starving the hexosamine pathway of glucose and glutamine.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including UDP-GlcNAc measurements (Figure 1D) and L-PHA binding assays (Figure 1B).

claim: Reduced UDP-GlcNAc and N-glycan branching drives growth and pro-inflammatory TH17 over anti-inflammatory iTreg differentiation.
source: This drives growth and pro-inflammatory TH17 over anti-inflammatory-induced T regulatory (iTreg) differentiation, the latter by promoting endocytic loss of IL-2 receptor-α (CD25).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TH17/iTreg differentiation patterns (Figures 1F, 2E, 2F) and CD25 surface expression (Figure 2A-C).

claim: Reduced N-glycan branching promotes endocytic loss of IL-2 receptor-α (CD25) to drive TH17 over iTreg differentiation.
source: This drives growth and pro-inflammatory TH17 over anti-inflammatory-induced T regulatory (iTreg) differentiation, the latter by promoting endocytic loss of IL-2 receptor-α (CD25).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing CD25 surface retention (Figure 2A), endocytosis assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and IL-2 signaling (Figure 2D).

claim: Under anaerobic conditions, oxidative phosphorylation is blocked, forcing cells to generate ATP by converting glucose to lactate via glycolysis.
source: Under anaerobic conditions oxidative phosphorylation is blocked, forcing cells to generate ATP by converting glucose to lactate via glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: Glycolysis generates only 2 ATP per glucose instead of 36-38 ATP per glucose with complete oxidation.
source: This is a highly inefficient use of glucose, generating only 2 ATP per glucose instead of 36–38 ATP per glucose with complete oxidation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about ATP yield from different metabolic pathways.

claim: Rapidly dividing cells switch their metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis under aerobic conditions.
source: Yet under aerobic conditions, rapidly dividing cells such as T cells paradoxically switch their metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis, where glucose is fermented to lactate despite the presence of oxygen (Wang et al., 1976; Warburg et al., 1927; Warburg et al., 1924) and primary carbon flux into the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) is switched from glucose to glutamine (DeBerardinis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Wang et al., 1976; Warburg et al., 1927; Warburg et al., 1924; DeBerardinis et al., 2007).

claim: In aerobic glycolysis, glucose is fermented to lactate despite the presence of oxygen.
source: Yet under aerobic conditions, rapidly dividing cells such as T cells paradoxically switch their metabolism from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis, where glucose is fermented to lactate despite the presence of oxygen (Wang et al., 1976; Warburg et al., 1927; Warburg et al., 1924)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Warburg's original work and subsequent studies.

claim: Primary carbon flux into the TCA cycle is switched from glucose to glutamine during aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis.
source: primary carbon flux into the tricarboxylic acid cycle (TCA cycle) is switched from glucose to glutamine (DeBerardinis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DeBerardinis et al., 2007.

claim: Biosynthetic pathways account for less than 10% of the increase in glucose uptake induced by the Warburg effect.
source: However, these biosynthetic pathways account for <10% of the increase in glucose uptake induced by the Warburg effect (DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Hume et al., 1978), implying other critical functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to DeBerardinis et al., 2007 and Hume et al., 1978.

claim: Genetically blocking lactate production in lung cancer does not activate oxidative phosphorylation in vivo yet still induces disease regression.
source: This hypothesis is questioned by the observation that genetically blocking lactate production in lung cancer does not activate oxidative phosphorylation in vivo yet still induces disease regression (Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xie et al., 2014.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis has been suggested to promote pro-inflammatory IFNγ synthesis.
source: Indeed, aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis have recently been suggested to promote pro-inflammatory IFNγ synthesis and TH1 differentiation (Chang et al., 2013; Gubser et al., 2013; Klysz et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2013; Gubser et al., 2013.

claim: Glutaminolysis has been suggested to promote TH1 differentiation.
source: Indeed, aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis have recently been suggested to promote pro-inflammatory IFNγ synthesis and TH1 differentiation (Chang et al., 2013; Gubser et al., 2013; Klysz et al., 2015), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klysz et al., 2015.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis promotes anti-tumor T cell activity.
source: Aerobic glycolysis also promotes anti-tumor T cell activity and differentiation into pro-inflammatory T helper 17 (TH17) over anti-inflammatory T regulatory (Treg) cells (Ho et al., 2015; Michalek et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2015; Michalek et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2011.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis promotes differentiation into pro-inflammatory TH17 over anti-inflammatory Treg cells.
source: Aerobic glycolysis also promotes anti-tumor T cell activity and differentiation into pro-inflammatory T helper 17 (TH17) over anti-inflammatory T regulatory (Treg) cells (Ho et al., 2015; Michalek et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2015; Michalek et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2011.

claim: Branched N-glycans bind galectins at the cell surface to simultaneously inhibit the endocytosis and signaling of multiple surface receptors and transporters.
source: Branched N-glycans bind galectins at the cell surface to simultaneously inhibit the endocytosis and signaling of multiple surface receptors and transporters, thereby controlling cell growth, differentiation and disease states such as autoimmunity, cancer and type 2 diabetes (Demetriou et al., 2001; Dennis et al., 2009; Granovsky et al., 2000; Lau et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011; Ohtsubo et al., 2005; Partridge et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work (Demetriou et al., 2001; Dennis et al., 2009; Granovsky et al., 2000; Lau et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011; Ohtsubo et al., 2005; Partridge et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2014).

claim: N-glycan branching regulates T cell development, growth, differentiation and autoimmunity.
source: In T cells, N-glycan branching regulates development, growth, differentiation and autoimmunity by altering T cell receptor clustering/signaling, surface retention/localization of CD4, CD8, CD45 and CTLA-4, and the differentiation into pro-inflammatory TH1 over anti-inflammatory TH2 cells (Chen et al., 2009, 2007; Demetriou et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2007; Morgan et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2009, 2007; Demetriou et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2007; Morgan et al., 2004; Zhou et al., 2014).

claim: De novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc begins with the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to glucosamine-6-phosphate by GFPT.
source: De novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc, the sugar-nucleotide donor substrate required by the N-glycan branching Golgi enzymes Mgat1, 2, 4 and 5, begins with the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to glucosamine-6-phosphate by the rate-limiting enzyme glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase (GFPT, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: GFPT is the rate-limiting enzyme for UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis.
source: De novo synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc, the sugar-nucleotide donor substrate required by the N-glycan branching Golgi enzymes Mgat1, 2, 4 and 5, begins with the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to glucosamine-6-phosphate by the rate-limiting enzyme glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase (GFPT, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the hexosamine pathway.

claim: GFPT requires glutamine as an amine donor to generate glucosamine-6-phosphate from fructose-6-phosphate.
source: GFPT also requires glutamine as an amine donor to generate glucosamine-6-phosphate from fructose-6-phosphate.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about GFPT enzyme function.

claim: The hexosamine pathway may be in direct competition with glycolysis and glutaminolysis for fructose-6-phosphate and glutamine, respectively.
source: Thus, the hexosamine pathway may be in direct competition with glycolysis and glutaminolysis for fructose-6-phosphate and glutamine, respectively.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the shared substrates between pathways, which forms the basis of the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: TH17 inducing cytokines (TGFβ+IL-6+IL-23) act synergistically to markedly reduce L-PHA binding in activated T cells by approximately 3-4 fold.
source: Strikingly, TH17 inducing cytokines (TGFβ+IL-6+IL-23) acted synergistically to markedly reduce L-PHA binding in activated T cells by ~3–4 fold, despite each cytokine individually having minimal effects (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each TH17 cytokine individually has minimal effects on L-PHA binding.
source: Strikingly, TH17 inducing cytokines (TGFβ+IL-6+IL-23) acted synergistically to markedly reduce L-PHA binding in activated T cells by ~3–4 fold, despite each cytokine individually having minimal effects (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TH17 inducing cytokines significantly reduce binding of E-PHA while increasing the binding of ConA.
source: Consistent with reduced branching TH17 inducing cytokines also significantly reduced binding of E-PHA (Phaseolus vulgaris, erthroagglutinin) while increasing the binding of ConA (Concanavalin A), plant lectins that bind bisecting and high-mannose N-glycans, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TH17 inducing cytokines markedly reduce the binding of galectin-3 to activated T cells.
source: Reduced branching should also decrease galectin binding and indeed, TH17 inducing cytokines markedly reduced the binding of galectin-3 to activated T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only approximately 20% change in branching is sufficient to alter T cell growth.
source: As only a ~20% change in branching is sufficient to alter T cell growth (Lee et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014), the reduction induced by TH17 inducing cytokines is highly significant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Lee et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).

claim: mRNA expression of Mgat1 and Mgat5 are unchanged or increased by TH17 cytokines.
source: Although branching was reduced, mRNA expression of the Golgi branching genes Mgat1 and Mgat5 were unchanged or increased, consistent with reduced UDP-GlcNAc supply being primarily responsible for lowering branching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: T cell activation markedly increases protein expression of GFPT1, HK1, GPI and PFK1 isoenzymes.
source: Indeed, while T cell activation markedly increases protein expression of GFPT1 as well as the critical glycolytic enzymes HK1, GPI and PFK1 isoenzymes (liver, platelet and muscle), GFPT1 is uniquely and specifically down-regulated by TH17 cytokines (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GFPT1 is uniquely and specifically down-regulated by TH17 cytokines.
source: Indeed, while T cell activation markedly increases protein expression of GFPT1 as well as the critical glycolytic enzymes HK1, GPI and PFK1 isoenzymes (liver, platelet and muscle), GFPT1 is uniquely and specifically down-regulated by TH17 cytokines (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GFPT2 is not detectable by Western blot in T cells.
source: GFPT2 is an isoenzyme of GFPT1 but is not detectable by Western blot in T cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Western blot experiments, though the data is not shown.

claim: UDP-GlcNAc production is reduced by TH17 cytokines.
source: Indeed, UDP-GlcNAc production is reduced by TH17 cytokines (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation reverses the reduction in branching induced by TH17 cytokines.
source: Supplementing T cells with GlcNAc reversed the reduction in branching induced by TH17 cytokines and markedly inhibited TH17 differentiation (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation markedly inhibits TH17 differentiation.
source: Supplementing T cells with GlcNAc reversed the reduction in branching induced by TH17 cytokines and markedly inhibited TH17 differentiation (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation induces a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg cells despite the presence of TH17-inducing cytokines.
source: Remarkably, GlcNAc supplementation not only blocked TH17 differentiation but also induced a cell fate switch to iTreg cells, despite the presence of TH17-inducing cytokines (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GlcNAc is metabolically inert within cells and does not enter glycolysis, the TCA cycle or the pentose phosphate pathway.
source: GlcNAc is metabolically inert within cells and does not enter glycolysis, the TCA cycle or the pentose phosphate pathway (Wellen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wellen et al., 2010.

claim: Kifunensine blocks branching.
source: The mannosidase I inhibitor kifunensine (Figure 1A) blocks branching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Kifunensine reverses the effects of GlcNAc supplementation on TH17 and iTreg differentiation.
source: The mannosidase I inhibitor kifunensine (Figure 1A) blocks branching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and reversed the effects of GlcNAc supplementation, confirming that raising UDP-GlcNAc levels with GlcNAc supplementation blocked TH17 and promoted iTreg differentiation by restoring branching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis blocked disease progression.
source: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis, a model of multiple sclerosis, blocked disease progression, raised branching in T cells and suppressed TH17 in vivo (Grigorian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grigorian et al., 2011.

claim: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis raised branching in T cells.
source: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis, a model of multiple sclerosis, blocked disease progression, raised branching in T cells and suppressed TH17 in vivo (Grigorian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grigorian et al., 2011.

claim: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis suppressed TH17 in vivo.
source: Oral delivery of GlcNAc to mice with Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis, a model of multiple sclerosis, blocked disease progression, raised branching in T cells and suppressed TH17 in vivo (Grigorian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grigorian et al., 2011.

claim: Transgenic over-expression of Mgat5 induces a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg cells despite TH17-inducing cytokines.
source: Indeed, directly raising branching via transgenic over-expression of Mgat5 also induced a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg cells despite TH17-inducing cytokines (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Blocking branching with kifunensine significantly enhances TH17 induction.
source: Directly inhibiting branching should have the opposite effect of raising branching and indeed, blocking branching by culturing cells with kifunensine or by inducing deficiency of the branching enzymes Mgat1 (via doxycycline treatment of Mgat1f/ftetO-Cre+ROSArtTA mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Zhou et al., 2014) or Mgat5 (Mgat5-/-) (Demetriou et al., 2001) all significantly enhanced TH17 induction (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplements 1F and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Mgat1 deficiency significantly enhances TH17 induction.
source: Directly inhibiting branching should have the opposite effect of raising branching and indeed, blocking branching by culturing cells with kifunensine or by inducing deficiency of the branching enzymes Mgat1 (via doxycycline treatment of Mgat1f/ftetO-Cre+ROSArtTA mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Zhou et al., 2014) or Mgat5 (Mgat5-/-) (Demetriou et al., 2001) all significantly enhanced TH17 induction (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplements 1F and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Mgat5 deficiency significantly enhances TH17 induction.
source: Directly inhibiting branching should have the opposite effect of raising branching and indeed, blocking branching by culturing cells with kifunensine or by inducing deficiency of the branching enzymes Mgat1 (via doxycycline treatment of Mgat1f/ftetO-Cre+ROSArtTA mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Zhou et al., 2014) or Mgat5 (Mgat5-/-) (Demetriou et al., 2001) all significantly enhanced TH17 induction (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplements 1F and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: IL-2 suppresses TH17 and promotes iTreg differentiation.
source: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) suppresses TH17 and promotes iTreg differentiation (Davidson et al., 2007; Laurence et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2007 and Laurence et al., 2007.

claim: Mgat1 deletion markedly reduces surface expression and retention of CD25.
source: Blocking branching during TH17 induction via Mgat1 deletion markedly reduced surface expression and retention of CD25, the high-affinity alpha subunit of the IL-2 receptor (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation raises CD25 surface levels.
source: Up-regulation of branching via GlcNAc supplementation or Mgat5 over-expression had the opposite effect, raising CD25 surface levels (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Mgat5 over-expression raises CD25 surface levels.
source: Up-regulation of branching via GlcNAc supplementation or Mgat5 over-expression had the opposite effect, raising CD25 surface levels (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: IL-2 cytokine levels are not significantly altered by GlcNAc or kifunensine.
source: In contrast, IL-2 cytokine levels were not significantly altered by GlcNAc or kifunensine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: pSTAT5 signaling is markedly reduced by TH17 cytokines.
source: The IL-2 receptor signals via STAT5 and this is markedly reduced by TH17 cytokines (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation restores pSTAT5 signaling despite TH17 conditions.
source: GlcNAc supplementation restored pSTAT5 signaling despite TH17 conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sequestering endogenous IL-2 with anti-IL-2 antibody blocks the ability of GlcNAc to switch cell fate from TH17 to iTreg.
source: Sequestering endogenous IL-2 with anti-IL-2 antibody blocked the ability of GlcNAc to switch cell fate from TH17 to iTreg, suggesting that IL-2 is required for branching to promote iTreg over TH17 differentiation (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Inhibiting branching with Mgat1 deficiency blocks the ability of exogenous IL-2 to induce a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg.
source: Moreover, inhibiting branching with Mgat1 deficiency or kifunensine blocked the ability of exogenous IL-2 to induce a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Inhibiting branching with kifunensine blocks the ability of exogenous IL-2 to induce a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg.
source: Moreover, inhibiting branching with Mgat1 deficiency or kifunensine blocked the ability of exogenous IL-2 to induce a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Branching promotes surface retention of glucose transporters.
source: Branching promotes surface retention of glucose transporters (Lau et al., 2007; Ohtsubo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lau et al., 2007 and Ohtsubo et al., 2005.

claim: Glucose uptake under TH17-inducing conditions is enhanced by GlcNAc and inhibited by kifunensine.
source: Consistent with this, glucose uptake under TH17-inducing conditions was enhanced by GlcNAc and inhibited by kifunensine, as measured by intracellular staining for the glucose analog 2-NBDG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation does not significantly alter the glycolytic state of cells under TH17 inducing conditions at day 2 of culture.
source: Indeed, under TH17 inducing conditions, GlcNAc supplementation did not significantly alter the glycolytic state of the cells prior to differentiation, as measured by the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) at day 2 of culture (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analysis data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rapamycin lowers aerobic glycolysis, enhances branching and drives iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
source: Rapamycin and galactose both lowered aerobic glycolysis, enhanced branching and drove iTreg over TH17 differentiation (Figure 3B–G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-G.

claim: Galactose lowers aerobic glycolysis, enhances branching and drives iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
source: Rapamycin and galactose both lowered aerobic glycolysis, enhanced branching and drove iTreg over TH17 differentiation (Figure 3B–G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B-G.

claim: Mgat1 deficiency reverses the effects of rapamycin and galactose on iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
source: Importantly, the latter was reversed with Mgat1 deficiency or kifunensine (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), demonstrating that the increase in branching induced by blocking glycolysis was necessary to switch cell fate from TH17 to iTreg.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Kifunensine reverses the effects of rapamycin and galactose on iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
source: Importantly, the latter was reversed with Mgat1 deficiency or kifunensine (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D), demonstrating that the increase in branching induced by blocking glycolysis was necessary to switch cell fate from TH17 to iTreg.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Rapamycin has little effect on GFPT1 levels.
source: Rapamycin had little effect on GFPT1 levels, while galactose marginally increased GFPT1, consistent with glycolysis largely acting by metabolically limiting flux of fructose-6-phosphate to the hexosamine/branching pathway rather than altering enzyme expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Galactose marginally increases GFPT1 levels.
source: Rapamycin had little effect on GFPT1 levels, while galactose marginally increased GFPT1, consistent with glycolysis largely acting by metabolically limiting flux of fructose-6-phosphate to the hexosamine/branching pathway rather than altering enzyme expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Kifunensine does not reverse the inhibition of aerobic glycolysis induced by rapamycin and galactose.
source: Importantly, kifunensine did not reverse the inhibition of aerobic glycolysis induced by rapamycin and galactose (Figure 3B,C), establishing that TH17 differentiation does not require aerobic glycolysis beyond its effects on branching.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: 2-Deoxy-D-glucose reduces branching and promotes TH17 differentiation.
source: Indeed, 2-deoxy-D-glucose/2-deoxy-D-mannose reduced branching and promoted TH17 differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G), consistent with branching being dominant over aerobic glycolysis in controlling TH17 differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Branching inhibits T cell growth by reducing T cell receptor clustering/signaling and promoting surface retention of CTLA-4.
source: Branching inhibits T cell growth by reducing T cell receptor clustering/signaling and promoting surface retention of the growth inhibitor CTLA-4 (Demetriou et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Demetriou et al., 2001; Lau et al., 2007; Mkhikian et al., 2011).

claim: GFPT1 is markedly up-regulated in neutral T cell blasts.
source: However, in contrast to TH17 cells, GFPT1 is markedly up-regulated in neutral T cell blasts (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Rapamycin and galactose enhance branching and inhibit T cell growth under neutral conditions.
source: Indeed, rapamycin and galactose enhanced branching and inhibited T cell growth, effects reversed with the Golgi branching inhibitor kifunensine (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kifunensine reverses the effects of rapamycin and galactose on branching and T cell growth under neutral conditions.
source: Indeed, rapamycin and galactose enhanced branching and inhibited T cell growth, effects reversed with the Golgi branching inhibitor kifunensine (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: iTreg cells induced by TGFβ alone are non-glycolytic and utilize lipid oxidation for ATP production.
source: iTreg cells induced by TGFβ alone are non-glycolytic and utilize lipid oxidation for ATP production (Michalek et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Michalek et al., 2011 and Shi et al., 2011.

claim: Abolishing branching via Mgat1 deficiency virtually eliminates iTreg differentiation induced by TGFβ.
source: Indeed, abolishing branching via Mgat1 deficiency virtually eliminated iTreg differentiation induced by TGFβ (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: iTreg differentiation is inhibited by Mgat5 deficiency.
source: iTreg differentiation was also inhibited by Mgat5 deficiency and kifunensine (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: iTreg differentiation is inhibited by kifunensine.
source: iTreg differentiation was also inhibited by Mgat5 deficiency and kifunensine (Figure 4B,C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Raising branching with GlcNAc promotes iTreg differentiation.
source: while raising branching with GlcNAc had the opposite effect (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Etomoxir decreases branching, CD25 surface expression and iTreg generation.
source: Indeed, etomoxir decreased branching, CD25 surface expression and iTreg generation; phenotypes reversed by GlcNAc supplementation (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: GlcNAc supplementation reverses the effects of etomoxir on branching, CD25 surface expression and iTreg generation.
source: Indeed, etomoxir decreased branching, CD25 surface expression and iTreg generation; phenotypes reversed by GlcNAc supplementation (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Excess exogenous glutamine raises branching under TH17 conditions.
source: Indeed, under TH17 conditions excess glutamine raised branching, markedly inhibited TH17 differentiation and induced a cell fate switch to iTreg (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Excess exogenous glutamine markedly inhibits TH17 differentiation under TH17 conditions.
source: Indeed, under TH17 conditions excess glutamine raised branching, markedly inhibited TH17 differentiation and induced a cell fate switch to iTreg (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Excess exogenous glutamine induces a cell fate switch to iTreg under TH17 conditions.
source: Indeed, under TH17 conditions excess glutamine raised branching, markedly inhibited TH17 differentiation and induced a cell fate switch to iTreg (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kifunensine reverses the effects of excess glutamine on TH17 and iTreg differentiation.
source: These phenotypes were reversed by blocking branching with kifunensine, confirming that excess glutamine acted by raising branching.
evidence: This is implied by the data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Increasing glutamine under iTreg-inducing conditions raises branching and increases iTreg generation in the absence but not in the presence of kifunensine.
source: Similarly, increasing glutamine under iTreg-inducing conditions raised branching and increased iTreg generation in the absence but not in the presence of kifunensine (Figure 6C,D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C,D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DON enhances branching and induces a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg.
source: Indeed, both glutaminase inhibitors enhanced branching and induced a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg (Figure 6E–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E-J.

claim: Azaserine enhances branching and induces a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg.
source: Indeed, both glutaminase inhibitors enhanced branching and induced a cell fate switch from TH17 to iTreg (Figure 6E–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E-J.

claim: DMK does not reverse the effects of DON on branching or TH17 induction.
source: In contrast, we observed that DMK did not reverse the effects of glutaminase inhibition by DON on branching or TH17 induction (Figure 6E,G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E,G.

claim: DMK induces a partial rescue of iTreg generation in the presence of DON.
source: However, DMK did induce a partial rescue of iTreg generation (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Kifunensine only partially reverses the effects of DON and Azaserine on TH17 versus iTreg generation.
source: Moreover, blocking branching with kifunensine only partially reversed the effects of DON and Azaserine on TH17 versus iTreg generation (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G-J.

claim: Glutamine availability regulates branching to affect TH17 versus iTreg differentiation.
source: Together, these data indicate that glutamine availability regulates branching to affect TH17 versus iTreg differentiation, but other factors such as catabolism of glutamine to α-ketoglutarate likely also play a role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of glutamine manipulation on branching and differentiation (Figures 6A-J).

claim: Catabolism of glutamine to α-ketoglutarate likely plays a role in TH17 versus iTreg differentiation beyond effects on branching.
source: Together, these data indicate that glutamine availability regulates branching to affect TH17 versus iTreg differentiation, but other factors such as catabolism of glutamine to α-ketoglutarate likely also play a role.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue by DMK and kifunensine shown in Figures 6G-J.

claim: A primary function of aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis is to cooperatively limit metabolite supply to N-glycan biosynthesis.
source: Thus, a primary function of aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis is to co-operatively limit metabolite supply to N-glycan biosynthesis, an activity with widespread implications for autoimmunity and cancer.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the collective experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Reduced branching induced by aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis promotes pro-inflammatory TH17 differentiation over anti-inflammatory iTreg differentiation in T cells.
source: In T cells, reduced branching induced by aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis promotes pro-inflammatory TH17 differentiation over anti-inflammatory iTreg differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: Restoring branching and UDP-GlcNAc levels via salvage of GlcNAc does not alter the glycolytic state of the cell.
source: Restoring branching and UDP-GlcNAc levels via salvage of N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) into the hexosamine pathway does not alter the glycolytic state of the cell, yet switches cell fate from TH17 to iTreg cells by blocking endocytic loss of IL-2 receptor-α (CD25).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic data (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and differentiation data (Figure 1F).

claim: Forcing oxidative phosphorylation raises branching to drive iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
source: Forcing oxidative phosphorylation raises branching to drive iTreg over TH17 differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by data with rapamycin and galactose shown in Figures 3B-G.

claim: Blocking the increase in branching reverses the effects of forcing oxidative phosphorylation on TH17 versus iTreg differentiation.
source: Blocking the increase in branching reverses the latter phenotypes, demonstrating that aerobic glycolysis is not essential for T cell growth/differentiation control beyond regulation of branching.
evidence: This is supported by data showing kifunensine and Mgat1 deficiency reverse effects of metabolic modulators (Figures 3F,G, 5A-C).

claim: GlcNAc has been reported to promote glucose, glutamine, and fatty acid uptake in liver and/or adipose tissue via branching induced increases in surface retention of metabolite transporters.
source: GlcNAc has recently been reported to promote glucose, glutamine, and fatty acid uptake in liver and/or adipose tissue via branching induced increases in surface retention of metabolite transporters (Ryczko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ryczko et al., 2016.

claim: Modifying branching in T cells with GlcNAc or kifunensine alters glucose uptake.
source: Similarly, we observed that modifying branching in T cells with GlcNAc or kifunensine altered glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by 2-NBDG uptake data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GlcNAc or kifunensine do not acutely alter the metabolic state of the T cell as measured by oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate.
source: However, GlcNAc or kifunensine did not acutely alter the metabolic state of the T cell, as measured by the oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lowering branching does not alter UDP-GlcNAc levels in T cells.
source: Consistent with this, we have previously shown that lowering branching does not alter UDP-GlcNAc levels in T cells (Mkhikian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mkhikian et al., 2016.

claim: GlcNAc raises UDP-GlcNAc levels.
source: GlcNAc does raise UDP-GlcNAc levels, which may impact other glycan pathways such as O-glycans, O-GlcNAc or CMP-sialic scid, in addition to N-glycan branching.
evidence: This is supported by UDP-GlcNAc measurement data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The effects of GlcNAc on T cell differentiation are predominantly through branching rather than other pathways.
source: However, the effects of GlcNAc on T cell differentiation were reversed by directly blocking Golgi branching activity, confirming that the effects of raised UDP-GlcNAc were predominantly through branching rather than other pathways.
evidence: This is supported by data showing kifunensine reverses GlcNAc effects (Figures 1F, 4C).

claim: T cell differentiation can be decoupled from the metabolic state of the cell by manipulating branching.
source: In this manner, T cell differentiation can be decoupled from the metabolic state of the cell by manipulating branching.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing branching manipulation affects differentiation without changing metabolic state.

claim: The competition between PFK1 and GFPT for fructose-6-phosphate is essential for determining the extent of glucose flux into the hexosamine/branching pathways.
source: The competition between PFK1 and GFPT for fructose-6-phosphate is essential for determining the extent of glucose flux into the hexosamine/branching pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations about GFPT1 and PFK1 expression patterns.

claim: During TH17 differentiation, GFPT1 is down-regulated and PFK1 dominates, restricting glucose flux into the hexosamine pathway and lowering branching relative to neutral T cell blasts.
source: During TH17 differentiation, GFPT1 is down-regulated and PFK1 dominates, restricting glucose flux into the hexosamine pathway and lowering branching relative to neutral T cell blasts.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 1C) and branching measurements (Figure 1B).

claim: GFPT1 is up-regulated in neutral T cell blasts, allowing increases in glucose uptake to raise de novo UDP-GlcNAc production and branching relative to resting cells.
source: In contrast, GFPT1 is up-regulated in neutral T cell blasts, allowing increases in glucose uptake to raise de novo UDP-GlcNAc production and branching relative to resting cells (Lau et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 1C) and citation to Lau et al., 2007.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis in neutral T cell blasts functions to limit the extent of glucose flux into the hexosamine pathway and thereby promotes growth.
source: however, aerobic glycolysis still functions to limit the extent of glucose flux into the hexosamine pathway and thereby functions to promote growth.
evidence: This is supported by data showing rapamycin and galactose effects on growth (Figure 5A-C).

claim: Branching and Mgat5 are pathologically over-expressed in cancer cells.
source: The Warburg effect was first described in cancer cells, where branching and Mgat5 are pathologically over-expressed and serve as essential drivers of growth, motility and metastasis (Granovsky et al., 2000; Lau et al., 2007; Partridge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Granovsky et al., 2000; Lau et al., 2007; Partridge et al., 2004.

claim: N-glycan branching and the hexosamine pathway promote epithelial to mesenchymal transition and tumor growth by regulating surface expression of receptor tyrosine kinases and TGFβ receptors.
source: N-glycan branching and the hexosamine pathway promote epithelial to mesenchymal transition and tumor growth by regulating surface expression of receptor tyrosine kinases and TGFβ receptors (Demetriou et al., 1995; Lau et al., 2007; Partridge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Demetriou et al., 1995; Lau et al., 2007; Partridge et al., 2004.

claim: Oncogenes such as Kras have been reported to turn on hexosamine and N-glycan pathway genes.
source: While oncogenes such as Kras have been reported to turn on hexosamine and N-glycan pathway genes (Ying et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ying et al., 2012.

claim: GFPT expression is elevated in a number of cancers.
source: GFPT expression is elevated in a number of cancers (Itkonen et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2012) (R. Zhou and M. Demetriou, unpublished data)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Itkonen et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2012 and unpublished data.

claim: GlcNAc has been given orally (3-6 g/day) to children with refractory inflammatory bowel disease for approximately 2 years, with 8 of 12 showing clinical improvement without reported toxicities and/or side effects.
source: GlcNAc has also been given orally (3–6 g/day) to children with refractory inflammatory bowel disease for ~2 years, with 8 of 12 showing clinical improvement without reported toxicities and/or side effects (Salvatore et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salvatore et al., 2000.

claim: Serum levels of endogenous GlcNAc are markedly reduced in patients with the progressive form of MS and correlate with clinical disability and imaging measures of neurodegeneration.
source: We have recently observed that serum levels of endogenous GlcNAc are markedly reduced in patients with the progressive form of MS and correlate with clinical disability and imaging measures of neurodegeneration (Alexander Brandt and Michael Demetriou, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: A pilot study of low-dose oral GlcNAc in MS (3 g/day) increased serum GlcNAc levels and branching in T cells.
source: A pilot study of low-dose oral GlcNAc in MS (3 g/day) increased serum GlcNAc levels and branching in T cells (Barbara Newton and Michael Demetriou, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors.

claim: GlcNAc is a dietary supplement that is for sale 'over the counter' in the US.
source: As GlcNAc is a dietary supplement that is for sale 'over the counter' in the US, these data suggest that GlcNAc may serve as a safe and inexpensive therapeutic for MS patients and potentially other autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the regulatory status of GlcNAc.

claim: GlcNAc may serve as a safe and inexpensive therapeutic for MS patients and potentially other autoimmune diseases.
source: As GlcNAc is a dietary supplement that is for sale 'over the counter' in the US, these data suggest that GlcNAc may serve as a safe and inexpensive therapeutic for MS patients and potentially other autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and clinical observations mentioned.
